segs.e: Linked Discourses 20.1
1. Similes
A Roof Peak
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Buddha … said:

segs.p: “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kūṭāgārassa yā kāci gopānasiyo sabbā tā kūṭaṅgamā kūṭasamosaraṇā kūṭasamugghātā sabbā tā samugghātaṁ gacchanti;
segs.e: “Mendicants, the rafters of a bungalow all lean to the peak and meet at the peak, and when the peak is demolished they’re all demolished too.

segs.p: evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye keci akusalā dhammā sabbe te avijjāmūlakā avijjāsamosaraṇā avijjāsamugghātā, sabbe te samugghātaṁ gacchanti.
segs.e: In the same way all unskillful qualities are rooted in ignorance and meet in ignorance, and when ignorance is demolished they’re all demolished too.
So you should train like this:
‘We will stay diligent.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.2
1. Similes
A Fingernail
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā parittaṁ nakhasikhāyaṁ paṁsuṁ āropetvā bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: Then the Buddha, picking up a little bit of dirt on his fingernail, addressed the mendicants:
“What do you think, mendicants?

segs.p: katamaṁ nu kho bahutaraṁ, yo cāyaṁ mayā paritto nakhasikhāyaṁ paṁsu āropito yā cāyaṁ mahāpathavī”ti?
segs.e: Which is more: the little bit of dirt on my fingernail, or this great earth?”
“Sir, the great earth is far more.

segs.p: Appamattakoyaṁ bhagavatā paritto nakhasikhāyaṁ paṁsu āropito.
segs.e: The little bit of dirt on your fingernail is tiny.

segs.p: Saṅkhampi na upeti upanidhimpi na upeti kalabhāgampi na upeti mahāpathaviṁ upanidhāya bhagavatā paritto nakhasikhāyaṁ paṁsu āropito”ti.
segs.e: Compared to the great earth, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction.”

segs.p: “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, appakā te sattā ye manussesu paccājāyanti;
segs.e: “In the same way the sentient beings reborn as humans are few,

segs.p: atha kho eteyeva bahutarā sattā ye aññatra manussehi paccājāyanti.
segs.e: while those not reborn as humans are many.
So you should train like this:
‘We will stay diligent.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.3
1. Similes
Families
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yāni kānici kulāni bahutthikāni appapurisāni tāni suppadhaṁsiyāni honti corehi kumbhatthenakehi;
segs.e: “Mendicants, those families with many women and few men are easy prey for bandits and  grain-jar thieves.

segs.p: evameva kho, bhikkhave, yassa kassaci bhikkhuno mettācetovimutti abhāvitā abahulīkatā so suppadhaṁsiyo hoti amanussehi.
segs.e: In the same way any mendicant who has not developed and cultivated the heart’s release by love is easy prey for non-humans.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yāni kānici kulāni appitthikāni bahupurisāni tāni duppadhaṁsiyāni honti corehi kumbhatthenakehi;
segs.e: Those families with few women and many men are hard prey for bandits and grain-jar thieves.

segs.p: evameva kho, bhikkhave, yassa kassaci bhikkhuno mettācetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā so duppadhaṁsiyo hoti amanussehi.
segs.e: In the same way a mendicant who has developed and cultivated the heart’s release by love is hard prey for non-humans.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘mettā no cetovimutti bhāvitā bhavissati bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will develop the heart’s release by love. We’ll cultivate it, make it our vehicle and our basis, keep it up, consolidate it, and properly implement it.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.4
1. Similes
Cauldrons
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Yo, bhikkhave, pubbaṇhasamayaṁ okkhāsataṁ dānaṁ dadeyya, yo majjhanhikasamayaṁ okkhāsataṁ dānaṁ dadeyya, yo sāyanhasamayaṁ okkhāsataṁ dānaṁ dadeyya, yo vā pubbaṇhasamayaṁ antamaso gadduhanamattampi mettacittaṁ bhāveyya, yo vā majjhanhikasamayaṁ antamaso gadduhanamattampi mettacittaṁ bhāveyya, yo vā sāyanhasamayaṁ antamaso gadduhanamattampi mettacittaṁ bhāveyya, idaṁ tato mahapphalataraṁ.
segs.e: “Mendicants, suppose one person was to give a gift of a hundred cauldrons of rice in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. And someone else was to develop a heart of love, even just as long as it takes to pull a cow’s udder. The latter would be more fruitful.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘mettā no cetovimutti bhāvitā bhavissati bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will develop the heart’s release by love. We’ll cultivate it, make it our vehicle and our basis, keep it up, consolidate it, and properly implement it.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.5
1. Similes
A Spear
At Sāvatthī.
“Mendicants, suppose there was a sharp-pointed spear.
And a man came along and thought,

segs.p: ‘ahaṁ imaṁ sattiṁ tiṇhaphalaṁ pāṇinā vā muṭṭhinā vā paṭileṇissāmi paṭikoṭṭissāmi paṭivaṭṭessāmī’ti.
segs.e: ‘With my hand or fist I’ll fold this sharp spear over, crumple it, and bend it back!’
What do you think, mendicants?

segs.p: bhabbo nu kho so puriso amuṁ sattiṁ tiṇhaphalaṁ pāṇinā vā muṭṭhinā vā paṭileṇetuṁ paṭikoṭṭetuṁ paṭivaṭṭetun”ti?
segs.e: Is that man capable of doing so?”
“No, sir.
Why not?

segs.p: “Asu hi, bhante, satti tiṇhaphalā na sukarā pāṇinā vā muṭṭhinā vā paṭileṇetuṁ paṭikoṭṭetuṁ paṭivaṭṭetuṁ.
segs.e: Because it’s not easy to fold that sharp spear over, crumple it, and bend it back with the hand or fist.

segs.p: Yāvadeva ca pana so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti.
segs.e: That man will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

segs.p: “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yassa kassaci bhikkhuno mettācetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā, tassa ce amanusso cittaṁ khipitabbaṁ maññeyya;
segs.e: “In the same way, suppose a mendicant has developed the heart’s release by love, has cultivated it, made it a vehicle and a basis, kept it up, consolidated it, and properly implemented it. Should any non-human think to overthrow their mind,

segs.p: atha kho sveva amanusso kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assa.
segs.e: they’ll eventually get weary and frustrated.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘mettā no cetovimutti bhāvitā bhavissati bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will develop the heart’s release by love. We’ll cultivate it, make it our vehicle and our basis, keep it up, consolidate it, and properly implement it.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.6
1. Similes
The Archers
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, cattāro daḷhadhammā dhanuggahā susikkhitā katahatthā katūpāsanā catuddisā ṭhitā assu.
segs.e: “Mendicants, suppose there were four well-trained expert archers with strong bows standing in the four quarters.
And a man came along and thought,

segs.p: ‘ahaṁ imesaṁ catunnaṁ daḷhadhammānaṁ dhanuggahānaṁ susikkhitānaṁ katahatthānaṁ katūpāsanānaṁ catuddisā kaṇḍe khitte appatiṭṭhite pathaviyaṁ gahetvā āharissāmī’ti.
segs.e: ‘When these four well-trained expert archers shoot arrows in four quarters, I’ll catch them before they reach the ground, and then I’ll bring them back.’
What do you think, mendicants?
Are they qualified to be called ‘a speedster endowed with super-speed’?”

segs.p: “Ekassa cepi, bhante, daḷhadhammassa dhanuggahassa susikkhitassa katahatthassa katūpāsanassa kaṇḍaṁ khittaṁ appatiṭṭhitaṁ pathaviyaṁ gahetvā āhareyya:
segs.e: “If he could catch an arrow shot by just one well-trained expert archer before it reaches the ground and bring it back,

segs.p: ‘javano puriso paramena javena samannāgato’ti alaṁvacanāya, ko pana vādo catunnaṁ daḷhadhammānaṁ dhanuggahānaṁ susikkhitānaṁ katahatthānaṁ katūpāsanānan”ti?
segs.e: he’d be qualified to be called ‘a speedster endowed with super-speed’. How much more so arrows shot by four archers!”

segs.p: “Yathā ca, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa javo, yathā ca candimasūriyānaṁ javo, tato sīghataro.
segs.e: “As fast as that man is, the sun and moon are faster.

segs.p: Yathā ca, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa javo yathā ca candimasūriyānaṁ javo yathā ca yā devatā candimasūriyānaṁ purato dhāvanti tāsaṁ devatānaṁ javo, (…) tato sīghataraṁ āyusaṅkhārā khīyanti.
segs.e: As fast as that man is, as fast as the sun and moon are, and as fast as the deities that run before the sun and moon are, the waning of the life forces is faster.
So you should train like this:
‘We will stay diligent.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.7
1. Similes
The Drum Called Plugger
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, dasārahānaṁ ānako nāma mudiṅgo ahosi.
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, the Dasārahas had a mridangam drum called the Plugger.

segs.p: Tassa dasārahā ānake ghaṭite aññaṁ āṇiṁ odahiṁsu.
segs.e: When the Plugger cracked, the Dasārahas patched it with another plug.

segs.p: Ahu kho so, bhikkhave, samayo yaṁ ānakassa mudiṅgassa porāṇaṁ pokkharaphalakaṁ antaradhāyi.
segs.e: Eventually, there came a time when the old wooden shell for the drumskin disappeared
and all that was left of the mridangam Plugger was a mass of plugs.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhavissanti bhikkhū anāgatamaddhānaṁ, ye te suttantā tathāgatabhāsitā gambhīrā gambhīratthā lokuttarā suññatappaṭisaṁyuttā, tesu bhaññamānesu na sussūsissanti na sotaṁ odahissanti na aññā cittaṁ upaṭṭhāpessanti na ca te dhamme uggahetabbaṁ pariyāpuṇitabbaṁ maññissanti.
segs.e: In the same way, in a future time there will be mendicants who won’t want to listen when discourses spoken by the Realized One—deep, profound, transcendent, dealing with emptiness—are being recited. They won’t actively listen or try to understand, nor will they think those teachings are worth learning and memorizing.

segs.p: Ye pana te suttantā kavikatā kāveyyā cittakkharā cittabyañjanā bāhirakā sāvakabhāsitā, tesu bhaññamānesu sussūsissanti, sotaṁ odahissanti, aññā cittaṁ upaṭṭhāpessanti, te ca dhamme uggahetabbaṁ pariyāpuṇitabbaṁ maññissanti.
segs.e: But when discourses composed by poets—poetry, with fancy words and phrases, composed by outsiders or spoken by disciples—are being recited they will want to listen. They’ll actively listen and try to understand, and they’ll think those teachings are worth learning and memorizing.

segs.p: Evametesaṁ, bhikkhave, suttantānaṁ tathāgatabhāsitānaṁ gambhīrānaṁ gambhīratthānaṁ lokuttarānaṁ suññatappaṭisaṁyuttānaṁ antaradhānaṁ bhavissati.
segs.e: And that is how the discourses spoken by the Realized One—deep, profound, transcendent, dealing with emptiness—will disappear.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘ye te suttantā tathāgatabhāsitā gambhīrā gambhīratthā lokuttarā suññatappaṭisaṁyuttā, tesu bhaññamānesu sussūsissāma, sotaṁ odahissāma, aññā cittaṁ upaṭṭhāpessāma, te ca dhamme uggahetabbaṁ pariyāpuṇitabbaṁ maññissāmā’ti.
segs.e: ‘When discourses spoken by the Realized One—deep, profound, transcendent, dealing with emptiness—are being recited we will want to listen. We will actively listen and try to understand, and we will think those teachings are worth learning and memorizing.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.8
1. Similes
Wood Blocks
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā vesāliyaṁ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṁ.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:

segs.p: “Kaliṅgarūpadhānā, bhikkhave, etarahi licchavī viharanti appamattā ātāpino upāsanasmiṁ.
segs.e: “Mendicants, these days the Licchavis live using wood blocks as pillows, and they exercise diligently and keenly.

segs.p: Tesaṁ rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto na labhati otāraṁ na labhati ārammaṇaṁ.
segs.e: King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, finds no vulnerability, he’s got no opportunity.

segs.p: Bhavissanti, bhikkhave, anāgatamaddhānaṁ licchavī sukhumālā mudutalunahatthapādā
segs.e: But in the future the Licchavis will become delicate, with soft and tender hands and feet.

segs.p: te mudukāsu seyyāsu tūlabibbohanāsu yāvasūriyuggamanā seyyaṁ kappissanti.
segs.e: They’ll sleep on soft beds with down pillows until the sun comes up.

segs.p: Tesaṁ rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto lacchati otāraṁ lacchati ārammaṇaṁ.
segs.e: King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, will find a vulnerability and get an opportunity.

segs.p: Kaliṅgarūpadhānā, bhikkhave, etarahi bhikkhū viharanti appamattā ātāpino padhānasmiṁ.
segs.e: These days the mendicants live using wood blocks as pillows, and they meditate diligently and keenly.

segs.p: Tesaṁ māro pāpimā na labhati otāraṁ na labhati ārammaṇaṁ.
segs.e: Māra the Wicked finds no vulnerability, he’s got no opportunity.

segs.p: Bhavissanti, bhikkhave, anāgatamaddhānaṁ bhikkhū sukhumā mudutalunahatthapādā.
segs.e: But in the future the mendicants will become delicate, with soft and tender hands and feet.

segs.p: Te mudukāsu seyyāsu tūlabibbohanāsu yāvasūriyuggamanā seyyaṁ kappissanti.
segs.e: They’ll sleep on soft beds with down pillows until the sun comes up.

segs.p: Tesaṁ māro pāpimā lacchati otāraṁ lacchati ārammaṇaṁ.
segs.e: Māra the Wicked will find a vulnerability and get an opportunity.
So you should train like this:
‘We will live using wood blocks as pillows, and we will meditate diligently and keenly.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.9
1. Similes
A Bull Elephant
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena aññataro navo bhikkhu ativelaṁ kulāni upasaṅkamati.
segs.e: Now at that time a certain junior mendicant went to visit families too often.
The mendicants said to him,
“Venerable, don’t go to visit families too often.”
But that mendicant, when spoken to by the mendicants, said this,

segs.p: “ime hi nāma therā bhikkhū kulāni upasaṅkamitabbaṁ maññissanti, kimaṅgaṁ panāhan”ti?
segs.e: “But these senior mendicants think they can go to visit families, so why can’t I?”

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: And then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened. The Buddha said:

segs.p: “idha, bhante, aññataro navo bhikkhu ativelaṁ kulāni upasaṅkamati.
‘ime hi nāma therā bhikkhū kulāni upasaṅkamitabbaṁ maññissanti, kimaṅgaṁ panāhan’”ti.

segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, there was a great lake in the jungle,
with bull elephants living nearby.

segs.p: Te taṁ sarasiṁ ogāhetvā soṇḍāya bhisamuḷālaṁ abbuhetvā suvikkhālitaṁ vikkhāletvā akaddamaṁ saṅkhāditvā ajjhoharanti.
segs.e: They’d plunge into the lake and pull up lotus bulbs with their trunks. They’d wash them thoroughly until they were free of mud before chewing and swallowing them.

segs.p: Tesaṁ taṁ vaṇṇāya ceva hoti balāya ca, na ca tatonidānaṁ maraṇaṁ vā nigacchanti maraṇamattaṁ vā dukkhaṁ.
segs.e: That was good for their appearance and strength, and wouldn’t result in death or deadly pain.

segs.p: Tesaṁyeva kho pana, bhikkhave, mahānāgānaṁ anusikkhamānā taruṇā bhiṅkacchāpā taṁ sarasiṁ ogāhetvā soṇḍāya bhisamuḷālaṁ abbuhetvā na suvikkhālitaṁ vikkhāletvā sakaddamaṁ asaṅkhāditvā ajjhoharanti.
segs.e: The young calves, following the example of the great bull elephants, plunged into the lake and pulled up lotus bulbs with their trunks. But they didn’t wash them thoroughly, and while they were still muddy they chewed and swallowed them.

segs.p: Tesaṁ taṁ neva vaṇṇāya hoti na balāya.
segs.e: That was not good for their appearance and strength, and resulted in death or deadly pain.

segs.p: Tatonidānaṁ maraṇaṁ vā nigacchanti maraṇamattaṁ vā dukkhaṁ.
Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idha therā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṁ vā nigamaṁ vā piṇḍāya pavisanti.
segs.e: In the same way, there are senior mendicants who robe up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, enter the town or village for alms.
There they speak on the teachings,
and lay people demonstrate their confidence in them.

segs.p: Te taṁ lābhaṁ agadhitā amucchitā anajjhopannā ādīnavadassāvino nissaraṇapaññā paribhuñjanti.
segs.e: And when they get things, they use them untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape.

segs.p: Tesaṁ taṁ vaṇṇāya ceva hoti balāya ca, na ca tatonidānaṁ maraṇaṁ vā nigacchanti maraṇamattaṁ vā dukkhaṁ.
segs.e: That’s good for their appearance and strength, and doesn’t result in death or deadly pain.

segs.p: Tesaṁyeva kho pana, bhikkhave, therānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ anusikkhamānā navā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṁ vā nigamaṁ vā piṇḍāya pavisanti.
segs.e: Junior mendicants, following the example of the senior mendicants, robe up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, enter the town or village for alms.
There they speak on the teachings,
and lay people demonstrate their confidence in them.

segs.p: Te taṁ lābhaṁ gadhitā mucchitā ajjhopannā anādīnavadassāvino anissaraṇapaññā paribhuñjanti.
segs.e: But when they get things, they use them tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, not understanding the escape.

segs.p: Tesaṁ taṁ neva vaṇṇāya hoti na balāya, te tatonidānaṁ maraṇaṁ vā nigacchanti maraṇamattaṁ vā dukkhaṁ.
segs.e: That’s not good for their appearance and strength, and results in death or deadly pain.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘agadhitā amucchitā anajjhopannā ādīnavadassāvino nissaraṇapaññā taṁ lābhaṁ paribhuñjissāmā’ti.
segs.e: ‘When we get things, we will use them untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.10
1. Similes
A Cat
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena aññataro bhikkhu ativelaṁ kulesu cārittaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: Now at that time a certain mendicant had relations with families too often.
The mendicants said to him,
“Venerable, don’t have relations with families too often.”

segs.p: So bhikkhu bhikkhūhi vuccamāno na viramati.
segs.e: But that mendicant, when spoken to by the mendicants, did not stop.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: And then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened. The Buddha said:

segs.p: “idha, bhante, aññataro bhikkhu ativelaṁ kulesu cārittaṁ āpajjati.
So bhikkhu bhikkhūhi vuccamāno na viramatī”ti.
“Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, biḷāro sandhisamalasaṅkaṭīre ṭhito ahosi mudumūsiṁ maggayamāno:
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a cat was standing by an alley or a drain or a dustbin hunting a little mouse, thinking,

segs.p: ‘yadāyaṁ mudumūsi gocarāya pakkamissati, tattheva naṁ gahetvā khādissāmī’ti.
segs.e: ‘When that little mouse comes out to feed, I’ll catch it right there and eat it!’

segs.p: Atha kho so, bhikkhave, mudumūsi gocarāya pakkāmi.
segs.e: And then that little mouse came out to feed.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ biḷāro gahetvā sahasā saṅkhāditvā ajjhohari.
segs.e: The cat caught it and hastily swallowed it without chewing.

segs.p: Tassa so mudumūsi antampi khādi, antaguṇampi khādi.
segs.e: But that little mouse ate its intestines and mesentery,

segs.p: So tatonidānaṁ maraṇampi nigacchi maraṇamattampi dukkhaṁ.
segs.e: resulting in death and deadly pain.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco bhikkhu pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṁ vā nigamaṁ vā piṇḍāya pavisati arakkhiteneva kāyena arakkhitāya vācāya arakkhitena cittena, anupaṭṭhitāya satiyā, asaṁvutehi indriyehi.
segs.e: In the same way, take a certain monk who robes up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, enters the village or town for alms without guarding body, speech, and mind, without establishing mindfulness, and without restraining the sense faculties.

segs.p: So tattha passati mātugāmaṁ dunnivatthaṁ vā duppārutaṁ vā.
segs.e: There he sees a lady scantily clad, with revealing clothes.

segs.p: Tassa mātugāmaṁ disvā dunnivatthaṁ vā duppārutaṁ vā rāgo cittaṁ anuddhaṁseti.
segs.e: Lust infects his mind,

segs.p: So rāgānuddhaṁsena cittena maraṇaṁ vā nigacchati maraṇamattaṁ vā dukkhaṁ.
segs.e: resulting in death or deadly pain.

segs.p: Maraṇañhetaṁ, bhikkhave, ariyassa vinaye yo sikkhaṁ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattati.
segs.e: For it is death in the training of the Noble One to resign the training and return to a lesser life.

segs.p: Maraṇamattañhetaṁ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṁ yadidaṁ aññataraṁ saṅkiliṭṭhaṁ āpattiṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: And it is deadly pain to commit one of the corrupt offenses
for which rehabilitation is possible.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘rakkhiteneva kāyena rakkhitāya vācāya rakkhitena cittena, upaṭṭhitāya satiyā, saṁvutehi indriyehi gāmaṁ vā nigamaṁ vā piṇḍāya pavisissāmā’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will enter the village or town for alms guarding body, speech, and mind, establishing mindfulness, and restraining the sense faculties.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.11
1. Similes
A Jackal
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Assuttha no tumhe, bhikkhave, rattiyā paccūsasamayaṁ jarasiṅgālassa vassamānassā”ti?
segs.e: “Mendicants, did you hear an old jackal howling at the crack of dawn?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Eso kho, bhikkhave, jarasiṅgālo ukkaṇḍakena nāma rogajātena phuṭṭho.
segs.e: “That old jackal has the disease called mange.

segs.p: So yena yena icchati tena tena gacchati;
segs.e: Yet it still goes where it wants,

segs.p: yattha yattha icchati tattha tattha tiṭṭhati;
segs.e: stands where it wants,

segs.p: yattha yattha icchati tattha tattha nisīdati;
segs.e: sits where it wants,

segs.p: yattha yattha icchati tattha tattha nipajjati;
segs.e: and lies down where it wants.
And the cool breeze still blows on it.

segs.p: Sādhu khvassa, bhikkhave, yaṁ idhekacco sakyaputtiyapaṭiñño evarūpampi attabhāvapaṭilābhaṁ paṭisaṁvediyetha.
segs.e: A certain person here who claims to follow the Sakyan would be lucky to experience even such an incarnation.
So you should train like this:
‘We will stay diligent.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 20.12
1. Similes
A Jackal (2nd)
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Assuttha no tumhe, bhikkhave, rattiyā paccūsasamayaṁ jarasiṅgālassa vassamānassā”ti?
segs.e: “Mendicants, did you hear an old jackal howling at the crack of dawn?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Siyā kho, bhikkhave, tasmiṁ jarasiṅgāle yā kāci kataññutā kataveditā, na tveva idhekacce sakyaputtiyapaṭiññe siyā yā kāci kataññutā kataveditā.
segs.e: “There might be some gratitude and thankfulness in that old jackal, but there is none in a certain person here who claims to follow the Sakyan.
So you should train like this:
‘We will be grateful and thankful.

segs.p: na ca no amhesu appakampi kataṁ nassissatī’ti.
segs.e: We won’t forget even a small thing done for us.’
That’s how you should train.”
The Linked Discourses with similes are complete.
